example_words.cultural_context: A basic Russian question word often learned first
A common phrase built from the Russian word for “what”

thoughts: In this word, the initial ч sounds like “sh,” not the usual “ch.” The word is common in Russian but unlikely to be familiar to English speakers who have not studied Russian.
description: Start with “sht,” rather than “cht”: say “sh” as in “shoe,” immediately followed by “t.” Stress the first syllable. The final ы is a Russian vowel with no exact English equivalent; keep your tongue farther back than for “ee.”

example_words.cultural_context: A very common Russian word used to express purpose.

thoughts: At the end of a word, тся is pronounced like ца; the spelling does not indicate three separate sounds.
description: Say “ts” as in “cats,” followed by a short, unstressed “uh.” Don’t pronounce a separate “y” sound.

example_words.cultural_context: Used in the common beginner phrase meaning “I like it.”

thoughts: At the end of an infinitive, ться is pronounced like ца; the ь does not make a separate sound.
description: Say “tsuh,” with the “ts” from “cats” followed by a short, unstressed “uh.” Do not pronounce it as separate “t” and “sya” sounds.

example_words.cultural_context: Related to photography and photographs
Related to training and exercise
Used in the common Russian phrase meaning “I like it”

thoughts: At the end of adjectives and pronouns, ого is usually pronounced with a v sound instead of g. In other words, such as the country name Того, the g sound remains.
description: In words like того and Большого, say v instead of g: roughly “tuh-VOH” and “buhl-SHOH-vuh.” In the country name Того, pronounce the g: roughly “tuh-GOH.”

example_words.cultural_context: As in the name of the famous Bolshoi Theatre
The West African country
A common Russian pronoun, included to contrast with the country name

thoughts: At the end of common Russian pronouns, его is pronounced with a v sound. In borrowed names, the г usually keeps its g sound.
description: In его meaning “him” or “his,” say roughly “yee-VOH”: the г sounds like English v, not g. In names such as Лего and Сан-Диего, pronounce г like the g in “go.”

example_words.cultural_context: A basic Russian pronoun
The familiar toy-brick brand
The well-known California city

thoughts: The ending is pronounced with a Russian vowel that English lacks, followed by a brief y-like glide. It is usually unstressed in the examples below.
description: Say ы with your tongue pulled back, rather than using the English “ee” sound, then finish with a short “y” glide. In everyday speech, the unstressed ending is quite brief.

example_words.cultural_context: The first word of Красный Октябрь, or Red October
The color in the name of a White Russian cocktail

thoughts: At the end of a word, ий is usually unstressed and follows a softened consonant.
description: Say a short “ee” followed by a very light “y” glide, as if beginning the word “yes.” Keep the preceding consonant soft; do not pronounce ий as English “eye.”

example_words.cultural_context: First name of cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin
Surname of the famous composer

thoughts: At the end of familiar Russian names and loanwords, ой is usually stressed and sounds much like English “oy.” When unstressed, it is shorter and less distinct.
description: Pronounce ой like the “oy” in “boy”: start with an “aw”-like sound and glide toward “y.” In an unstressed ending, say it more lightly.

example_words.cultural_context: Surname of the author of War and Peace
The Bolshoi Theatre is famous for ballet
The familiar figure from Western films
An English loanword also used in Russian

thoughts: At the end of a word, ая is usually unstressed, but its а can also carry the stress. These examples show both.
description: Pronounce it as two sounds: roughly “uh-yuh” when unstressed, or “AH-yuh” when the а is stressed. Keep the brief y sound between the vowels.

example_words.cultural_context: The first word in the Russian name for Red Square; ая is unstressed
The first word in the Russian name for Hagia Sophia; the а in ая is stressed

thoughts: At the end of words such as синяя, the two letters я have different unstressed sounds. The first follows a soft consonant; the second begins with a y-like glide.
description: In these examples, say the first я roughly like the i in “bit,” then the second like a quick “yuh.” Keep the preceding consonant soft, with your tongue raised toward the roof of your mouth.

example_words.cultural_context: The word for the familiar color blue
Used when talking about places such as ancient Greece

thoughts: At the end of a word, ое sounds different depending on whether the о is stressed.
description: When stressed, ое sounds roughly like “OY-yeh.” When unstressed, the о weakens, making the ending closer to “uh-yuh.” Keep the vowels light rather than pronouncing them as two strong English syllables.

example_words.cultural_context: Related to the familiar name Bolshoi, as in the Bolshoi Ballet
A familiar food; the Russian word has an unstressed ending
The first word in the Russian name for the Red Sea

thoughts: At the end of these words, the first е is stressed and the second is unstressed.
description: Say the first е like “yeh,” then glide into a short, unstressed “yih.” Keep the sounds connected rather than pronouncing two equally strong syllables.

example_words.cultural_context: An inflected form of the familiar place name Korea
An inflected form of the familiar word museum
An inflected form of the familiar word idea

thoughts: At the end of a Russian word, б is pronounced like English p because final voiced consonants are devoiced.
description: Pronounce final б like the p in “cup,” not the b in “cub.” Close your lips and release them without voicing.

example_words.cultural_context: Same meaning as the familiar English word “club.”
The familiar sea animal.
The familiar grilled meat dish.

thoughts: At the end of a Russian word, written в is normally pronounced like English f, not v.
description: Pronounce final в like the f in “off.” For example, the last sound of Чехов is f, even though the spelling ends in в.

example_words.cultural_context: Famous Russian playwright and short-story writer
Former Soviet leader
Capital of Ukraine

thoughts: At the end of a Russian word, г is normally pronounced like English k, even though it usually sounds like g elsewhere.
description: Pronounce final г like the k in “back,” not the g in “bag.” This change is called final devoicing.

example_words.cultural_context: The familiar word for an online blog
The familiar fast-food item
The Soviet prison-camp system; its first г sounds like g, but its final г sounds like k

thoughts: At the end of a Russian word, written д is normally pronounced like т because final voiced consonants become voiceless.
description: Pronounce final д like the ‘t’ in ‘cat,’ not the ‘d’ in ‘bad.’ Keep the sound short and crisp.

example_words.cultural_context: The famous American film industry and its home in Los Angeles
The famous Disney theme park
A familiar term for quick-service food

thoughts: At the end of a Russian word, ж is pronounced as a voiceless ш sound.
description: Pronounce final ж roughly like the “sh” in “shoe,” not the “zh” sound in “vision.” Keep your tongue slightly farther back than for English “sh.”

example_words.cultural_context: The same everyday place as an English garage
The same treatment as an English massage
The same kind of artwork as an English collage

thoughts: At the end of a Russian word, з is pronounced like English s, not z.
description: Pronounce final з like the s in “bus.” Russian devoices it at the end of a word, even though it is written з.

example_words.cultural_context: The familiar music genre
A word closely related to English “gas”
The mountain region often mentioned in geography and news

thoughts: The letters тс form a /ts/ cluster that English speakers already use in words like “cats.”
description: Say a quick t followed immediately by s, like the ending of “cats.” Keep both sounds together, without adding a vowel between them.

example_words.cultural_context: Sherlock Holmes’s famous companion
The title character of The Great Gatsby
A country in southern Africa

thoughts: The д loses its voicing before с, so the pair sounds approximately like “ts.” It often occurs before к in familiar adjectives.
description: Pronounce дс roughly like the “ts” in “cats,” not like English “ds.” Before к, the result sounds like “tsk,” with no vowel between the consonants.

example_words.cultural_context: An adjective referring to Hollywood films
An adjective referring to Sweden
The familiar water sport

thoughts: The two letters дж usually represent one sound, familiar from English words such as “jazz” and “jam.”
description: Pronounce дж like the English “j” in “jazz”: begin with a “d” closure and release into the sound of “zh” in “measure.” In some words, especially across word boundaries, the letters may be pronounced separately.

example_words.cultural_context: The same music genre known in English
A familiar word for a small electronic device
A familiar type of educational institution

thoughts: The spelling дз occurs in familiar Russian names and loanwords. It can sound like a firm “dz” or a softened “dz” before ю or и.
description: Say “d” and “z” together, like the ending of English “beds.” Before ю or и, soften it by raising the middle of your tongue toward the roof of your mouth.

example_words.cultural_context: Zen Buddhism is widely known in English.
The Olympic martial art.
The famous movie monster.

thoughts: The spelling сч usually represents one prolonged soft “sh” sound, rather than separate “s” and “ch” sounds. Widely familiar Russian names and loanwords containing this exact spelling are rare, so the examples use everyday concepts.
description: Usually pronounced like a longer, softer English “sh.” Keep the middle of your tongue raised toward the roof of your mouth, and do not pronounce a separate “s.”

example_words.cultural_context: A common word for happiness in Russian greetings and songs
Used for sports scores and restaurant bills

thoughts: The spelling зч is uncommon. In the examples below, the two letters combine into one long, soft sound rather than being pronounced separately.
description: Pronounce зч like a prolonged “sh,” with the middle of your tongue raised toward the roof of your mouth. Do not say a separate “z” or the “ch” in “chair.”

example_words.cultural_context: A horse-drawn cab driver in historical Russia
Contains джаз, the Russian word for jazz

thoughts: The letters жч usually merge into one prolonged soft “sh” sound. Russian words containing this exact spelling are unlikely to be familiar to most English speakers.
description: Pronounce жч as a slightly longer, softer “sh,” with your tongue raised toward the roof of your mouth. In мужчина, do not pronounce a separate “zh” followed by “ch.”

example_words.cultural_context: A basic Russian word for an adult man.

thoughts: The letters т and ч usually merge into a single “ch” sound. Common loanwords provide familiar examples.
description: Pronounce тч much like “ch” in English “match,” not as a separate “t” followed by “ch.” In some Russian words, the sound is held slightly longer.

example_words.cultural_context: Common sports term, borrowed from English
Familiar tomato condiment
An English loanword for a short comedy scene or drawing

thoughts: This spelling occurs in words for familiar concepts, but the Russian words themselves are unlikely to be familiar to most English speakers.
description: Usually pronounced like a slightly prolonged English “ch” in “church.” The д blends into the following ч; do not pronounce it as a separate “d.”

example_words.cultural_context: A familiar role in international conversations
A familiar figure from spy stories

thoughts: In ordinary words, сш usually merges into a long ш sound. In the abbreviation США, the letters are pronounced separately.
description: In ordinary words, pronounce сш like a slightly longer English “sh,” without inserting a vowel. In abbreviations such as США, say the letter names separately instead.

example_words.cultural_context: The idea of deciphering a code is familiar from spy stories.
The Russian abbreviation for the United States; its letters are said separately.

thoughts: The spelling зж usually merges into a prolonged ж sound. Russian words containing it are unlikely to be familiar to most English speakers.
description: Usually pronounced as one long, voiced “zh” sound, rather than a separate z followed by zh. It resembles the sound in “measure,” but is held longer and made with the tongue slightly farther back.

example_words.cultural_context: A familiar digestive complaint, though the Russian word may be new.
A common description of a lifeless person or place.
Often used for lighting a fire.

thoughts: The doubled letters usually represent one prolonged sound, not two separate consonants. Russian words containing жж are unlikely to be familiar to most English speakers, so the examples use recognizable concepts.
description: Pronounce жж as a held version of the sound in English “measure.” Keep your voice on throughout, without restarting the sound. In some traditional pronunciations, it sounds slightly softer.

example_words.cultural_context: The yeast used to make bread rise
The sound made by bees
Sugar browned for caramel

thoughts: The т is usually silent in common Russian words containing стн, but it is pronounced when ст and н meet across a prefix boundary.
description: Usually pronounce стн like English “sn,” skipping the т. In words such as постнатальный, pronounce all three consonants: “st-n,” as in “postnatal.”

example_words.cultural_context: Russian title of the famous film and novel
Medical term closely matching English “postnatal”

thoughts: In common words containing здн, the written д is silent. The resulting з-н sequence may feel unusual to English speakers.
description: Usually pronounce здн like “zn,” skipping the written д. Keep the з voiced, like the z in “zoo,” then move directly to n.

example_words.cultural_context: A common word for holidays and celebrations in Russia
An everyday word meaning “late”

thoughts: In common words containing рдц, the д is silent. The remaining sounds are a Russian r followed by ц, pronounced like the “ts” in “cats.”
description: Pronounce рдц as рц: make a brief tapped or rolled r, then “ts.” Do not pronounce the д.

example_words.cultural_context: The Russian word for heart
Title of a well-known Bulgakov novella

thoughts: In the common word солнце, the written л is silent, so лнц is pronounced like нц. The examples show the same pronunciation.
description: The л is silent: pronounce нц as an English “n” followed by “ts,” as in “ants.”

example_words.cultural_context: The everyday word for the sun
The summer or winter solstice

thoughts: The most recognizable example is the common greeting здравствуйте. In this word, the first в in вств is silent.
description: In здравствуйте, pronounce вств approximately like “stv”: skip the first в. In other words, the first в may instead sound like “f” before the following “s,” giving “fstv.”

example_words.cultural_context: A common Russian greeting often taught to beginners

thoughts: The final soft sign is silent; it changes the consonant immediately before it.
description: At the end of a word, ь has no sound of its own. It makes the preceding consonant “soft”: raise the middle of your tongue toward the roof of your mouth as you say that consonant. Don’t add a separate “y” sound or an extra syllable.
